questions.q: Why doesn't a large language model inherently treat a developer's system prompt as more authoritative than the end user's message?
options: It does treat it that way, by design, with a cryptographic signature on the system prompt
The model only reads the system prompt once per day for performance reasons

Everything the model receives — system prompt, developer instructions, user input, retrieved content — arrives as one undifferentiated stream of tokens, with no built-in structural wall between instructions and data
System prompts are stored in a separate, read-only database table that user input cannot reach
questions.explain: Unlike a SQL engine that structurally separates query logic from bound data, an LLM predicts its next token from everything in its context window — nothing inherently privileges the developer's instructions over text that merely looks like an instruction.

questions.q: In the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, which category covers prompt injection?
options: LLM01
It isn't in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications at all
LLM09
LLM05
questions.explain: Prompt injection is LLM01, the top entry in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, covering both direct and indirect variants.

questions.q: What makes a prompt injection attempt specifically "direct" rather than "indirect"?
options: Direct injection always targets a RAG pipeline's vector database
Direct injection requires the attacker to have administrator credentials on the LLM application's backend
Direct injection only works against open-source models, never hosted API models
The attacker is the end user, submitting the malicious input through the model's normal, expected input channel — no special access is needed
questions.explain: Direct injection is the simplest case: the same text box every legitimate user types into becomes the delivery channel, with no elevated access required.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what's the most useful way to build detection for direct prompt injection attempts in application logs?
options: Maintain an exhaustive denylist of every known exact attack phrase ever published

Recognize recurring patterns — attempts to assert new authority over the conversation, requests to reveal hidden configuration, or role-play framing used to bypass a refusal — rather than memorizing exact attack strings
Ignore the user-input channel entirely and only monitor server logs for failed logins
Rely on the model to self-report whenever it has been successfully manipulated
questions.explain: New exact phrasings appear constantly, so pattern-level recognition — not a denylist of literal strings — is what holds up over time.

questions.q: Why does direct prompt injection become a materially bigger risk once a model is wired to take real actions (e.g., applying account credits or writing to a repository)?
options: It doesn't — the risk is identical whether the model can only chat or can also take action
Action-taking models are always hosted on less secure infrastructure than chat-only models
It becomes an attacker using natural language as the exploit payload to trigger a real-world action the developer never intended to authorize, not just an embarrassing or off-topic reply
Because action-taking models use a different, more vulnerable tokenizer
questions.explain: A chatbot leaking its system prompt is embarrassing; the same manipulation against an agent with tool access can produce an unauthorized real-world action.
